title: Squares of a Sorted Array
description: Square a sorted array and keep it sorted in O(n) by filling the output from both ends inward.

data.text: Given an integer array `nums` sorted in non-decreasing order, return an array of the squares of each number, also sorted in non-decreasing order.

**Input:** `nums = [-4, -1, 0, 3, 10]`

**Output:** `[0, 1, 9, 16, 100]`

**Explanation:** After squaring, `[16, 1, 0, 9, 100]` is unsorted; sorting it gives the output above.
Square every element, then sort. Correct and concise, but it costs O(n log n) and discards the sorted input for free.

data.title: Square then sort O(n log n)

data.text: The largest square must come from whichever end has the larger absolute value. Walk two pointers inward from the ends and fill the output array from the back, placing the larger square each time. Each step is O(1), so the whole thing is O(n).

data.title: Two Pointers O(n)
data.content: Compare absolute values at both ends, write the biggest square last.

data.title: Filling backwards is the key insight
data.text: You know the *largest* square before you know the smallest, so writing the output from the end turns an apparent sorting problem into a single linear merge of two sorted sequences — the negative half and the non-negative half.

data.title: Why the loop must use the value not index
data.text: The condition compares `leftSq > rightSq`, the squared values, not the raw values. Comparing `nums[left] > nums[right]` is wrong for negatives: `-4` is smaller than `3` but squares to a larger number.

data.caption: Both ends hold the candidates for the next largest square, so the output is filled right to left.

data.title: Complete solution
data.content: This is a merge problem in disguise: the squares of the negative prefix descend, the squares of the non-negative suffix ascend, and you merge them from the largest downwards. Recognising the merge is what removes the sort.
